system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the
step that takes the work, and the words, claim or court defect it turns on.

### The court defects in 99 F.Supp.3d 585

### Contract 99FSupp3d585_asset_purchase_and_product

#### c094 — 8.5(b)(iii) Transfer of Purchased Assets

```
ii) CollaGenex shall transfer to Skold the Purchased Assets and Additional Records relating to such terminated Products, Such transfer shall be accompanied by documentation, dala and information related to the Purchased Assets that can be transferred by CollaGenex:
```

- **d01** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The transfer command that CollaGenex “shall transfer to Skold the Purchased Assets” was vague because it specified no date, leaving unclear whether transfer was required immediately upon termination or at some later time.
  Opinion lines 103-103:
```
. The Court finds no merit in the Defendants’ argument that the breach accrued on the day Inc. terminated the 2004 Agreement. Section 8.2 of the Agreement expressly provided that Collagenex could terminate at any time after March 31, 2007. See Compl. Ex. A. Construing all reasonable inferences in the Plaintiff’s favor, the Agreement was unclear by what date Inc. was required to transfer assets to Skold after electing to terminate the Agreement. Any arguments to the contrary involve fact-specific issues of contract interpretation not appropriate for determination at this stage of the proceedings.
```

#### c100 — 9.1 Dispute Resolution; Mediation

```
9.1 Dispute Resolution; Mediation. Any dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof (each, a “Dispute”) shall first be referred by the Parties to their respective senior-level executives, or their designecs, {or attempted resolution through good faith negotiations. In the event that such persons cannot resolve the Dispute within thirty (30) days following either Party’s written request to initiate such negotiations, cither Party may, by written notice to the other, require that the Dispute be Teferred to non-binding mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association (the “AAA”) in accordance with its then-current Commercial Mediation Rules. The presiding mediator shall have experience with disputes involving the technology that is the subjcct matter of this Agreement, The mediation shall be conducted in the English language and all mediation sessions shall be held in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Parties shall each be responsible for one-half of any fees or other amounts payable to the AAA or the mediator, and each Party shal} bear its own attorneys’ fees and other expenses in connection with the mediation, If efforts at mediation are unsuccessful in resolving the Dispute within thirly (30) days after the first mediation session, either Party may pursue any and all legal or equitable remedies available to it, subject to the remaining provisions of this Agreement. The Parties agree that the procedures set forth in this paragraph shall be the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes. Notwithstanding the foregoing and subject to the remaining provisions of this Agreement, either 3 20en 1-PR/1256533.9 Party may seek injunctive or other equitable relief in a court of competent jurisdiction pending the outcome of any negotiations or mediation conducted hereunder.
```

- **d02** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The phrase “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require” mediation was disputed as either imposing mandatory mediation before suit or merely permitting a party to request nonbinding mediation, with the court adopting the permissive reading.
  Opinion lines 20-21:
```
The Defendants contend that the Complaint should be dismissed in its entirety for failure to comply with the 2004 Agreement’s dispute resolution and mediation clause. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. The clause provides that “[a]ny dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof shall first be referred by the parties to their senior-level executives for attempted resolution through good-faith negotiations.” Compl. Ex. A § 9.1 (emphasis added). Should negotiations fail, thirty days after making a written request to initiate those negotiations, “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require that the Dispute be referred to non-binding mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association.” Id. (emphasis added). The Defendants assert that Skold did not refer a dispute to a senior-level executive for negotiations and failed to make a written request that the dispute be referred to nonbinding mediation. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. Skold responds that the language of the mediation clause is permissive (“either Party may ... require”) and also argues that, in any event, Inc. has waived its right to invoke the clause because it participated in litigation over the dispute in the cancellation action before the TTAB. See Pl.’s L.P./Inc. Opp’n at 14-15.
The dispute resolution clause in the 2004 Agreement contains two clauses, one of which is mandatory (the parties shall refer the matter to senior executives to attempt to negotiate a resolution) and the other which is permissive (the parties may refer the matter to nonbinding mediation). Given the voluntary nature of the latter, this Court agrees with Skold that he was not required to refer this dispute to mediation before bringing suit here against Inc.
```

#### c109 — 9.10 Governing Law

```
9.10 Governing Law, This Agreement shall be governed and construed in accordance with the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, without giving effect to any choicc of law provisions thercof. Each Party hereby submits itself for the purpose of this Apreement and any controversy arising hereunder to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, and any courts of appeal therefrom, and waives any objection on the grounds of lack of jurisdiction (including, without limitation, venue) to the exercise of such jurisdiction over it by any such courts,
```

- **d03** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The scope of “any controversy arising hereunder” was disputed as potentially limited to contractual claims, but the court construed it to cover noncontractual claims that arise from the contractual relationship and implicate the Agreement’s terms.
  Opinion lines 82-88:
```
Forum selection clauses are treated as ordinary contract provisions and are subject to the ordinary rules of contract interpretation. See M/S Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co., 407 U.S. 1, 92 S.Ct. 1907, 32 L.Ed.2d 513 (1972). First, a court must determine whether the clause states the parties’ intentions unambiguously. “To be ‘unambiguous,’ a contract clause must be reasonably capable of only one construction.” Otto v. Erie Ins. Exch., 11 F.Supp.3d 482, 483 (E.D.Pa.2014). The' only reasonable construction of the clause in the 2004 Agreement (“Each Party hereby submits itself for the purpose of this Agreement and any controversy arising hereunder to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania ....”) is that any dispute between the parties arising under the Agreement must be litigated in Pennsylvania. This clause on its face is unambiguous. See Health Robotics, LLC v. Bennett, No. 09-0627, 2009 WL 1708067, at *3 (E.D.Pa. June 16, 2009). Having so found, this Court must now determine whether Skold’s claims “arise out of the Agreement” and are thus covered by the terms of the forum selection clause. Id.; see also Terra Int’l, Inc. v. Miss. Chem. Corp., 119 F.3d 688, 692 (8th Cir.1997) (stating that before a court can consider enforcing a forum selection clause, “it must first decide whether the clause applies to the type of claims asserted in the lawsuit”).
The Third Circuit’s decision in Crescent International v. Avatar Communities, Inc., 857 F.2d 943 (3d Cir.1988) (per cu-riam), is instructive on this question. The issue in Crescent involved interpretation of a forum selection clause in an agreement between Crescent, a Pennsylvania-based corporation, and Avatar, a Florida-based corporation, under which Crescent sold real estate owned by Avatar in return for commissions. The agreement chose Florida law and provided that “any litigation upon any of [its] terms ... shall be maintained” in a state or federal court in Miami, Florida. Id. at 944. Crescent, however, filed an action in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania alleging breach of contract and several related, albeit noncontractual, claims. Avatar moved to dismiss, arguing that the forum selection clause applied to noncontractual as well as contractual claims and, as such, the action was in the wrong forum. The district court agreed and dismissed the suit.
Crescent argued on appeal that the forum selection clause was narrowly drafted and could not apply to noncontractual claims. The Third Circuit, however, determined that the pleading of alternate non-contractual theories does not alone allow a party to avoid enforcement of a forum selection clause “if the claims asserted arise out of the contractual relation and implicate the contract’s terms.” Id. at 945. The court held that the district court correctly construed the forum selection clause, concluding that “[although only one of Crescent’s claims is based on a breach of contract theory, all of them involve allegations arising out of the agreement implicating its terms.” Id.; see also Coastal Steel Corp. v. Tilghman Wheelabrator Ltd., 709 F.2d 190, 203 (3d Cir.1983) (“[W]here the relationship between the parties is contractual, the pleading of alternative non-contractual theories of liability should not prevent enforcement of such a bargain.”), overruled on other grounds by Lauro Lines s.r.l. v. Chasser, 490 U.S. 495, 109 S.Ct. 1976, 104 L.Ed.2d 548 (1989).
Several decisions involving similarly worded forum selection clauses in similar factual scenarios from courts in other jurisdictions are also helpful in resolving this question. In Omron Healthcare, Inc. v. Maclaren Exports Ltd., 28 F.3d 600 (7th Cir.1994), the Seventh Circuit expressed its broad view on the applicability of forum selection clauses to claims, holding that “all disputes the resolution of which arguably depend on the construction of an agreement ‘arise out of that agreement” for purposes of enforcing such clauses. Id. at 603. In Laserdynamics, Inc. v. Acer America Corp., 209 F.R.D. 388 (S.D.Tex.2002), the Southern District of Texas held that important to the forum selection clause analysis was a determination of the “spirit” of the underlying agreement, as well as the subject matter comprising the agreement’s “nucleus.” Id. at 391. And finally, the Southern District of New York, in finding that a plaintiffs action “clear[ly]” arose pursuant to the contract and enforcing a forum selection clause, looked to the fact that the plaintiffs “entire business relation with the defendant ... stemmed from the contract,” and, as a result “[a]ny determination with respect to plaintiffs claims will require consideration of the contract and of the parties’ respective rights pursuant to the contract.” YWCA v. HMC Entm’t, Inc., No. 91-7943, 1992 WL 279361, at *4 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 25, 1992).
Taking into account the above analysis, the Court finds that the forum selection clause in the 2004 Agreement applies to Skóld’s claims against S.A. Those claims arise out of the 2004 Agreement and implicate its terms. See Crescent, 857 F.2d at 945. In fact, Skóld’s “entire business relation” with the Galder-ma entities with respect to the Restora-derm trademark stems from the 2004 Agreement. YWCA, 1992 WL 279361, at *4. Thus, determination of Skóld’s claims implicate the contract’s terms and will require consideration of the contract and the parties’ respective rights pursuant to the contract. See id. The 2004 Agreement is not “merely one of the final manifestations” of the “ongoing business relationships between the parties” — a situation in which forum selection clauses have been held inapplicable to noncontractual claims. Gen. Envtl. Sci. Corp. v. Horsfall, 753 F.Supp. 664, 667-68 (N.D.Ohio 1990). Quite the contrary, the 2004 Agreement was the final manifestation of the relationship between Skold and Collagenex and the only manifestation of a relationship between Skold and any Galderma entity.
The “nucleus” of the 2004 Agreement is the transfer of the Restoraderm trademark, and the “spirit of the ... agreement contemplate^] the rights and duties of the parties” concerning the Restoraderm trademark. Laserdynamics, 209 F.R.D. at 389. Accordingly, if any of the rights or obligations in the 2004 Agreement were “threatened or impaired by an act of the parties or their privities, that act gives rise to a dispute under the agreement.” Id. Skold’s allegations that the acts of the Defendants, in declining to revert the Res-toraderm intellectual property to him upon termination of the 2004 Agreement and continuing to market and sell products bearing the Restoraderm mark, are the nucleus of his claims that his rights under the 2004 Agreement have been impaired. S.A. should be expected to answer to those claims.
At bottom, because “all disputes the resolution of which arguably depend on the construction of an agreement ‘arise out of that agreement” for purposes of enforcing a forum selection clause, Omron, 28 F.3d at 603, the Court holds that S.A. cannot avoid enforcement of the forum selection clause because the non-contractual claims asserted “arise out of the contractual relation and implicate the contract’s terms.” Crescent, 857 F.2d at 945. When the substance of the plaintiffs claims, stripped of their labels, fall within the scope of the forum selection clause, the opposing party cannot avoid it. The dispute between Skóld and S.A. arises out of the 2004 Agreement”such that the forum selection clause is applicable against S.A. on all claims Skold has alleged.
```


### The items to rate

#### a01

On `99FSupp3d585_asset_purchase_and_product` c094 — 8.5(b)(iii) Transfer of Purchased Assets. Court defects on this provision: d01.

The description:
```
The subsection speaks of Purchased Assets "relating to such terminated Products," but paragraph (b) is triggered only by termination "in whole" under Section 8.2, so there is no antecedent set of terminated Products. Which assets must be transferred on a whole-agreement termination is left unstated.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d01.

#### a02

On `99FSupp3d585_asset_purchase_and_product` c100 — 9.1 Dispute Resolution; Mediation. Court defects on this provision: d02.

The description:
```
The clause declares the negotiation-and-mediation procedures "the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes" immediately after providing that a Party may pursue "any and all legal or equitable remedies" if mediation fails. The exclusivity sentence and the remedies sentence cannot both be given full effect.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d02.

#### a03

On `99FSupp3d585_asset_purchase_and_product` c109 — 9.10 Governing Law. Court defects on this provision: d03.

The description:
```
The submission to the exclusive jurisdiction of Pennsylvania courts sits against Section 9.1's statement that negotiation and mediation are "the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes." Which provision governs access to the courts must be worked out between the two.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d03.
